\begin{column}{0.265\textwidth}

\begin{block}{VISUAL ABSTRACT}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_chain.pdf}\\[6pt]
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_coverage.pdf}
\vspace{2pt}
\raggedright\footnotesize
Any matrix carrying the graph's pattern collapses to one linear recurrence of
order $2k+2$ --- the same number as the best known upper bound --- so the matrix
method has a ceiling that exactly meets the target. Reaching it with a
\emph{fixed} matrix can only ever settle $n$ in one divisibility class (blue),
and we prove that restriction is forced. Building the matrix out of \emph{tiles}
instead removes it: green marks the values now determined, and at $k=2,3$ that
is \textbf{every $n$}.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{INTRODUCTION}
\textbf{The forcing rule.} Colour some vertices of a graph. If a coloured
vertex has exactly one uncoloured neighbour, that neighbour becomes coloured.
Repeat. $Z(G)$ is the size of the smallest starting set that eventually
colours everything.

\textbf{Why it matters.} $Z(G)$ bounds the \emph{maximum nullity} $M(G)$: the
largest null space of a symmetric matrix carrying the graph's pattern. The
parameter arose independently in quantum control and in power-network sensor
placement.

\textbf{The family.} $P(n,k)$: outer $n$-cycle $u_iu_{i+1}$, inner edges
$v_iv_{i+k}$, spokes $u_iv_i$. Cubic on $2n$ vertices, rotation
$\rho: i\mapsto i+1$.

\textbf{The general object.} $P(n,k)$ is a \emph{cyclic cover}: a base graph
$B$ with edge voltages in $\mathbb Z_n$ lifts to $V(B)\times\mathbb Z_n$. Two
vertices, loops of voltage $1$ and $k$, a spoke of voltage $0$ --- that is
$P(n,k)$. Everything below is really about covers.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{PROBLEM FRAMING}
Exact values of $Z(P(n,k))$ were known only for $k=2$ and $k=3$. A
\textbf{July 2026} correction note (arXiv:2607.19412) exists because a
published 2020 theorem is \emph{false}: it claimed $Z(P(n,3))=8$ for $n\ge12$,
but $Z(P(12,3))=7$ --- the case analysis never tested $7$-vertex sets. That note
closes with:
\vspace{4pt}
\keybox{\itshape ``Determining $Z(P(n,k))$ for general $k$ --- the stabilization
threshold and a rigorous lower bound for $k\ge4$ --- remains open.''}
\vspace{4pt}

\textbf{The asymmetry.} Upper bounds are easy --- exhibit one forcing set. Lower
bounds must rule out \emph{every} smaller set.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{RESEARCH OBJECTIVES}
\begin{enumerate}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
\item Find the exact ceiling of the matrix-certificate method here.
\item Decide whether it can be attained, and construct certificates that do.
\item Determine \textbf{why} such certificates only ever settle $n$ in a
      divisibility class --- and escape it.
\item Obtain $Z(P(n,k))$ for \textbf{all large $n$}, certified, not extrapolated.
\item Report which $k$ and $n$ are settled, and which are not.
\end{enumerate}
\end{block}

\begin{block}{WHY STANDARD METHODS FAIL}
A set is forcing iff it meets every \emph{fort}. Three standard consequences
all fail here, and all degrade as $k$ grows:
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{3pt}
\item \textbf{Disjoint forts:} at most \emph{two} exist in any case tested.
\item \textbf{Fort LP:} integrality gap $\approx2$ ($\mathrm{LP}=3.21$ against
      $Z=10$ for $P(18,4)$) --- which also explains why fort-based solvers
      scale poorly here.
\item \textbf{Spectral:} Hoffman-type bound gives $1.2$--$2.9$ against true $Z$
      of $6$--$12$.
\end{itemize}
Insufficient \emph{in principle}, not merely in practice --- which is what
motivated changing the category of argument.
\end{block}

\end{column}

%% ======================= COLUMN 2 =======================
\begin{column}{0.435\textwidth}

\begin{block}{MATHEMATICAL METHODOLOGY}

\begin{columns}[t]
\begin{column}{0.49\textwidth}
\panel{1. The colour change rule and the rotation bootstrap}{figures/fig_forcing.pdf}{1.0}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.49\textwidth}
\panel{2. Support of the reduced recurrence: nine terms, order $2k+2$}{figures/fig_recurrence.pdf}{1.0}
\end{column}
\end{columns}

\vspace{6pt}
\textbf{Step 1 --- Reduction.} Every spoke weight $c_i$ is nonzero, so the kernel
equation at $u_i$ solves for $y_i=-(b'_{i-1}x_{i-1}+a_ix_i+b_ix_{i+1})/c_i$.
Substituting into the equation at $v_i$ leaves \emph{one scalar recurrence} in
$x$, supported on nine indices with both end coefficients nonzero.

\keybox{\textbf{Theorem 1 (Reduction).} For every matrix $A$ whose off-diagonal
support is exactly $E(P(n,k))$ --- symmetric \emph{or not} ---
\[
  \operatorname{null}A=\dim\ker(T-I)\ \le\ 2k+2 ,
\]
$T$ the monodromy of that order-$(2k+2)$ recurrence, with equality iff $T=I$.
The order $2k+2$ is exactly the size of the forcing set the rotation bootstrap
produces: \textbf{the ceiling of the method equals the upper bound it is trying
to match.}}

\vspace{6pt}
\textbf{Step 2 --- The symbol.} For $A$ invariant under $\rho$, the Fourier
blocks are $M_m=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a+s_m&c\\ c&d+et_m\end{smallmatrix}\right)$
with $s_m=2\cos\frac{2\pi m}{n}$. Since $t=L_k(s)$ exactly, where $L_k$ is the
monic integer polynomial with $L_k(z+z^{-1})=z^k+z^{-k}$,
\[
  \operatorname{null}A=\#\{m: F(s_m)=0\},\qquad
  F(s)=(s+a)L_k(s)+\alpha s+\beta .
\]
$F$ is monic of degree $k+1$ but carries \textbf{exactly three free
parameters, for every $k$}.

\vspace{4pt}
\keybox{\textbf{The key idea.} Three roots can be prescribed and no more --- but
prescribing three \emph{determines the other $k-2$}, and if $F$ has
\textbf{rational coefficients} its roots form Galois orbits, which stay inside
$\Gamma_n$. One rational $F$ places all $k+1$ roots at once.}

\vspace{4pt}
\textbf{Step 3 --- Cyclotomic construction.} Let $\Psi_d$ be the minimal
polynomial of $2\cos(2\pi/d)$, degree $\varphi(d)/2$. Choose distinct $d$'s with
$\sum\deg\Psi_d=k+1$, put $F=\prod\Psi_d$, and impose the $k-2$ integer
membership conditions. Every root then lies in $\Gamma_n$ for \emph{every} $n$
divisible by $\operatorname{lcm}(D)$. This gives \textbf{integer} certificates
--- e.g.\ $Z(P(n,4))=10$ for $60\mid n$ --- but only on that one class.

\vspace{6pt}
\keybox{\textbf{Theorem 2 (why the classes are forced).} A period-one symbol is
a \emph{fixed} polynomial; its roots are fixed algebraic numbers, and
$2\cos(2\pi j/d)$ lies on $\Gamma_n$ \emph{iff} $d\mid n$. So one such matrix
settles exactly $\{n:\operatorname{lcm}(D)\mid n\}$ --- a single class,
containing \textbf{at most one prime}. Worse, for $k\ge3$ every symbol obeys
$e_2=-k$, a Conway--Jones relation on the grid. For $k=2$ that coefficient is
free, \emph{which is exactly why $k=2$ alone was ever general in $n$.}}

\vspace{4pt}
\textbf{Step 4 --- Escape.} Theorem 1 characterises the ceiling for
\emph{every} matrix on the pattern by $T=I$, a condition with no arithmetic in
it. So stop using rotation-invariant matrices and build the weight sequence out
of \textbf{tiles}.

\vspace{4pt}
\panel{4. Tiles compose because their ends are pinned}{figures/fig_tiling.pdf}{1.0}

\vspace{4pt}
\keybox{\textbf{Theorem 3 (tiling).} $T_i$ depends only on weights within
$2k+2$ of position $i$. Pin a \textbf{docking pattern} on the first and last
$k+1$ positions of every tile: each tile's product then depends on its interior
alone, and $T=\prod T_{\rm tile}$. Hence \emph{identity tiles of every length in
$[L,2L)$ give $Z(P(n,k))=2k+2$ for every $n\ge L$} --- because every $n\ge L$ is
a sum of such lengths. \textbf{All large $n$ reduces to a finite list of finite
problems.}}
\end{block}

\begin{block}{RESULTS \& CERTIFICATION}
\keybox{\textbf{Main result.} Every value below is new or corrects a published one.
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 \multicolumn{2}{l}{Z(P(n,2)),\ Z(P(n,3))\ \text{and}\ Z(P(n,4))\
   \text{determined for \textbf{every} } n,}\\[3pt]
 \multicolumn{2}{l}{Z(P(n,3))=8 \ \text{exactly for } n\ge13,\ \text{and } 13
   \text{ is optimal}:\ Z(P(11,3))=Z(P(12,3))=7,}\\[3pt]
 \multicolumn{2}{l}{Z(P(n,4))=M(P(n,4))=10 \ \text{for every } n\ge\SettleFour,
   \quad Z(P(n,5))=M(P(n,5))=12 \ \text{for every } n\ge\SettleFive .}
\end{array}
\]
\textbf{We prove a conjecture stated in a July 2026 arXiv paper.} That note
found the 2020 error and closed with: \emph{``We conjecture $Z(P(n,3))=8$ for
$n\ge13$; the missing ingredient is a lower-bound proof valid for all large
$n$.''} The tiling construction is that missing ingredient.}

\vspace{4pt}
\textbf{How the three are proved.} $k=2$: the closed form
$c^2=-(s_1{+}s_2)(s_1{+}s_3)(s_2{+}s_3)$, positive at the three most negative
grid values for all $n\ge9$, $n\ne10$. $k=3,4$: Theorem 3 with $L=21$ and
$L=\SettleFour$, from \textbf{\NtileAll\ certified identity tiles} covering
$[21,43]$ at $k=3$, $[29,61]$ at $k=4$ and $[54,75]$ at $k=5$; below $L$, $k=3$ is closed by $17$ consecutive individually certified
values, and the remaining small $n$ by exhaustive search --- at $k=4$ that search
is exact up to the rotation symmetry and reaches $n=28$, which is what closes the
last gap.

\vspace{6pt}
\keybox{\textbf{Certifying a tile without interval arithmetic on a rational
map.} $T_{\rm tile}=I$ is rational in the weights. But by Theorem 1 the
monodromy of the \emph{one-tile} cyclic matrix \emph{is} the tile product, so
\[
 T_{\rm tile}=I \iff \operatorname{null}A_{\rm one\ tile}=2k+2,
\]
and a nullity is certified by the \textbf{bilinear} system $A(w)K(X)=0$, whose
Jacobian is affine. A \textbf{Krawczyk contraction bound} then proves a true
real solution exists in an explicit box. All $\NtileAll$ pass,
$\alpha\le\MaxAlpha$ --- and the test is evaluated in \textbf{exact rational arithmetic},
not float: the box centre is dyadic, $f$ and $J$ have integer coefficients, and
$Y$ may be any matrix, so $\alpha<1$ is an exact integer comparison.}

\vspace{4pt}
\textbf{The subtlety that makes it a proof.} $AK=0$ has rank $2nr-\binom r2$,
and the deficiency is structural: $K^{\!\top}\!AK$ is symmetric because $A$ is,
and $\binom r2$ is its antisymmetric part. Choosing the square subsystem
\emph{structurally} --- non-pivot rows plus the upper triangle of the pivot block
--- makes it \textbf{equivalent} to $AK=0$; choosing it by pivoting leaves
$\binom r2$ equations unproved, and the Krawczyk test still passes. Those
equations fall to $10^{-61}$ \emph{without being solved for}.

\vspace{4pt}
\textbf{Integer certificates, as a by-product.} With $a=\alpha=0$ the matrix is
the adjacency matrix with one spoke set \emph{negated}; its nullity is
classified by $Q_k(z)=z^{2k+2}+z^{2k}+z^{k+1}+z^2+1$, which splits into
cyclotomics only for $k=2,3,7$ --- giving $Z(P(n,7))=\mathbf{16}$ for $120\mid n$
from a matrix of $0,\pm1$.
\end{block}

\end{column}

\begin{column}{0.265\textwidth}

\begin{block}{VERIFICATION}
\textbf{One script re-derives everything.} \texttt{verify\_all.py}: $\Nchecks$ checks,
all passing --- the realisability theorem symbolically for $k=2..10$, every
integer certificate, all $\NtileAll$ tiles re-evaluated for nullity \emph{and} exact
docking, the claim that every $n$ in range is a sum of certified lengths, and
three Krawczyk contractions \emph{re-run in exact arithmetic}. It also checks the
poster's and paper's own numbers against the certificates on disk, so a stale
count fails the suite.

\textbf{Structural theorem:} $189$ random matrices over $63$ pairs $(n,k)$.
All pass.

\textbf{Engine validation:} the exhaustive $Z$ solver reproduced \emph{every}
published value first, including the corrected $Z(P(12,3))=7$.

\textbf{Triangulation.} The $n=17$ certificate was located three independent
ways --- minimising $\|T-I\|$, an alternating solve, and a fully gauge-fixed
search --- all yielding a Krawczyk-certified matrix. Stage~1 is only a search;
stages~2--3 are the proof, so the route does not enter the result.

\vspace{4pt}
\keybox{\textbf{Why a failed search proves nothing here.} \emph{Lemma.} Every
symmetric matrix on the pattern is gauge-equivalent to one in the slice we
search. So a failure inside it measures effort, not impossibility --- and this
bit: $P(18,3)$ and the tile $\ell=21$ were both reported as failures and both
succeeded once the restart budget was raised. \emph{Working rule: quote the
residual and the budget, never just ``failed''.}}
\end{block}

\begin{block}{CONCLUSIONS}
\begin{enumerate}\setlength{\itemsep}{4pt}
\item The method has an \textbf{exact ceiling of $2k+2$}, coinciding with the
      best known upper bound: either it settles $Z$ completely or nothing does.
\item {\color{provedc}\bfseries Proved:} $Z(P(n,2))$ and $Z(P(n,3))$
      and $Z(P(n,4))$ all \textbf{determined for every $n$}; and
      $Z(P(n,5))=12$ for every $n\ge\SettleFive$.
      \textbf{No divisibility conditions.} The $k=3$ sequence is
      $6,6,6,8,7,7,8,8,\dots$ --- non-monotone, which is how the published
      proof went wrong.
\item {\color{provedc}\bfseries Proved:} the congruence conditions of the
      cyclotomic layer were \emph{forced}, not a shortfall --- one class, at most
      one prime. That converts the earlier results into a demarcation.
\item {\color{provedc}\bfseries Proved:} $c^2=0$ iff the symbol factors as
      $(s+a)(L_k+t)$; over $\mathbb Q$, Niven's theorem caps the degenerate
      symbols at $25$ per $k$.
\item {\color{openc}\bfseries Corrected (my own), among others:} the claim this
      construction ``never exceeds $6$''; a false unconditional cover bound
      ($Z(P(8,2))=5$); the threshold $(2k+2)^2/5$; $N(k)=O(k)$; and an
      eigenvalue search whose negative results I \textbf{withdrew} after it
      reported nullity $7$ at $P(20,3)$ where $8$ is attained.
\end{enumerate}
\end{block}

\begin{block}{FUTURE WORK}
\textbf{Honest limits.} At $k=5$ the threshold $\SettleFive$ is \emph{not}
optimal: $\ell=73$ and $76\le\ell\le107$ are still unsolved, and filling them
would bring it down to $54$. $k\ge6$ has no tiles at all. $Z(P(n,4))$ is known
for every $n$, but the \emph{matrix} value $M(P(n,4))$ is still open at $n=24$
and $n=28$, where $Z=10$ but no certificate exists. The $k\ge6$
congruence-class values are numerical, a weaker standard than the rest. The rank
law is verified over a range, not proved.

\textbf{What we cannot diagnose.} We first searched $k=5$ over
$41\le\ell\le45$ --- the parameter count's bound --- and found nothing, then
found tiles starting near $54$. The count is a lower bound, \emph{not} a
predictor of where tiles begin ($21$ vs $16$ at $k=3$; $\approx54$ vs $41$ at
$k=5$), and we cannot explain the gap.

\textbf{Next.} Close $[54,108)$ for $k=5$ (mechanical); prove the rank law;
decide whether $M<Z$ strictly at $n=10$, $k=2$.
\end{block}
